label: Roto
notes: A session builds the whole engine (nothing shared between sessions), applies its limits, registers the host call function, then evaluates 1 + 1 and reads 2 back in Rust. Limits: none available: Roto has no instruction, time, or memory limit API; it is sandboxed by construction (only registered Rust functions and types are reachable, no I/O in the standard library).
Memory: resident growth across 1,000 live sessions (stopped by target), measured first in a fresh process.

Tool call: the guest calls a registered Rust function on its own stack. Median of per-batch means, 1,000,000 calls in batches of 1,000 after 100,000 warm-ups; mean 0.0523 µs, slowest batch 0.1162 µs per call; 0.0522 µs of CPU per call.
Roto is statically typed and JIT-compiled with Cranelift, so `1 + 1` means compiling `fn main() -> i64 { 1 + 1 }` to machine code: session = Runtime::from_lib(our library) + compile + call.

Roto has no maps, and its records cannot be passed to Rust functions, so the call argument is the closest structure: registered Rust types built by host constructors, call(Call.new(id, "lookup", Args.new("hello from the sandbox"))). That is three native calls per tool call (two constructors plus call); the reply is a registered Reply type read through native accessor methods (reply.id()).
Roto has no exceptions, so the guest counts id mismatches and the host asserts zero.
The tool-call loop is compiled machine code making three direct native calls per iteration, so it measures Roto's FFI and native-call cost rather than an interpreter.
Compute: not measured in the Rust host.
